extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers; undergraduate mathematics instructors interested in proof instruction and analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Use Toulmin's model to analyze instructor and student proof-writing/presentation in undergraduate mathematics (proof-based content courses), coding statements as data, warrant, backing, qualifier, or conclusion and comparing written vs spoken modeling. Applies to classroom observations, transcripts, and student written work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toulmin's six statement types
rubrics_metrics.description: Toulmin’s scheme has six basic types of statement, each of which play different roles in arguments: The data (D); The conclusion (C); The warrant (W); The backing (B); The modal qualifier (Q); The rebuttal (R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each element plays a distinct role in an argument and should be identified when analyzing proofs or proof-presentations. Use these categories as the primary coding taxonomy for statements in instructor and student proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Data (in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The data (D): the foundation upon which the argument is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational coding rule used in the study: a statement was classified as data if it directly followed 'if' or 'let' or was stated as an obvious fact without support (for example, f(0)=0 when discussing a homomorphism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Conclusion (in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusion (C): that which is being argued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational coding rule: a statement was classified as a conclusion when it followed 'then' or when it was presented as a deduction from a piece of data, such as 'R fulfills X property.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Warrant (in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The warrant (W): justifies the relationship between the data and the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational coding rule: a statement was classified as a warrant when it linked the data and conclusion in a way that explained how the data supported the conclusion and drew upon previously demonstrated facts or hypotheses (e.g., information about elements included in sets). Warrants may be written or spoken; their presence explains inferential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Backing (in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The backing (B): supports the warrant by suggesting why it is valid, or explains the permissibility of the warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational coding rule: a statement was classified as backing if it explained the applicability of a warrant such as the claim 'We have previously proved…'. Backing was often stated aloud but not written in the observed classroom examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Modal Qualifier (in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The modal qualifier (Q): expresses a degree of confidence of the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify qualifiers when statements limit generalizability or assert degrees of confidence; qualifiers were very rarely written by students or instructors in the observed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Rebuttal (in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rebuttal (R): states conditions under which the conclusion would not hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code rebuttals when the argument explicitly notes exceptions or counter-conditions; these were essentially absent in the observed written proofs in this study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for logging a 'proof-production or presentation' incident
rubrics_metrics.description: An incident was logged as such when any member of the class community wrote or showed a formal mathematical proof that drew on symbolic notation and logical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude informal justification unless it is at that moment connected to formal proof. Count work with particular examples as proof if algebraic techniques are being used. Prefer written work as modeling of proof-writing (it is more likely copied into notes), but include spoken modeling when it is connected to formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification rules for coding classroom statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify all written and spoken statements used in proof-writing as one of data, warrant, backing, qualifier or conclusion, with allowance that some statements may be introduced as conclusions and later reused as data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transcript and board text: data often follows 'if/let' or is obvious fact; conclusion often follows 'then'; warrants link data to conclusion; backing explains why warrant is permissible; qualifiers limit generalizability. Track whether each element is written, spoken, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for measuring written vs. spoken modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Record and transcribe classroom video; log episodes that include proof-writing or presentation; note for each Toulmin element whether the instructor wrote it, spoke it, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce frequency tables (e.g., counts of written Data, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, Conclusion; and counts when including spoken statements). Use these counts to characterize instructors' modeling behavior (e.g., Dr. Tripp: data and conclusions almost always written; warrants usually spoken but infrequently written; backing almost never written).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose proofs into top-level vs. property-verification arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish top-level arguments (the overall theorem/structure proof) from property-verification arguments (independent sub-arguments that verify particular properties required by the top-level claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze property-verification arguments separately because they often are more numerous and more accessible for analysis (e.g., showing a structure is a ring requires demonstrating multiple independent properties such as closure, identity, inverses, distributivity, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation linking instructor modeling to student writing
rubrics_metrics.description: If the instructor consistently writes certain argument elements, students are likely to write those elements; if the instructor inconsistently writes an element but states it aloud, students may show intermediate rates of writing that element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed frequencies to form expectations: because Dr. Tripp always wrote data and conclusions, students almost always wrote them; because she seldom wrote backing or qualifiers, students almost never wrote them; warrants were written by students at a rate between Dr. Tripp's written and spoken rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitivity of detail in student proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Students include more or less detail depending on familiarity with the operation or context: more unfamiliar operations elicit more written warrants/backing; highly familiar operations may be treated as self-evident and elicit less written detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing student work, compare across tasks (e.g., additive vs multiplicative properties) to see variation in inclusion of warrants/backing/qualifiers; do not treat uniform lack of warrants as necessarily a deficiency without considering task familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical recommendation: make modeling explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should make explicit statements (meta-dialogue) about the types of questions and levels of detail they expect students to include when writing proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example prompts suggested in the paper: 'Listen to the types of questions I ask you and ask myself. These are the kinds of things you should be asking while you write proofs.' or 'To decide when you should write down the answers to these questions you should …' Such explicit meta-instructions may increase students' inclusion of warrants and backing and decrease invalid proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding allowance for statements reused across roles
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex proofs some statements are first introduced as conclusions and then reused as data for a subsequent argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding, allow a single textual statement to be assigned different Toulmin roles at different points in the proof (conclusion in one subargument, data in the next). Record the role contextually rather than rigidly by literal phrasing alone.
